Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- The liver disease consists of two synchronous metastases, 2.2 cm (segment II) and 3 cm (segment V), both amenable to limited (segmental) resections.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on CT.  
- The primary tumour is symptomatic (obstruction) and therefore requires immediate treatment, but the patient has no reported comorbidities that would preclude combined surgery.  
- The planned hepatic resections would leave the majority of the liver parenchyma intact; even without a formal FLR calculation, removal of only segments II and V is a minor hepatectomy and is expected to preserve >30 % functional liver volume.  
- MDT already judged the metastases “primarily resectable.”  
These points satisfy the technical criteria for resectability (ability to achieve R0 resection while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and sufficient FLR), so surgery can be offered without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Urgent primary‑tumour control – Perform an oncologic left‑sided colectomy (standard left hemicolectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy) to relieve obstruction.  
2. Concurrent hepatic resection – In the same operative session, perform anatomical segmentectomy of segment II and non‑anatomical wedge resection of the lesion in segment V (or a combined left‑lateral and segment V resection) aiming for R0 margins. Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm lesion boundaries and exclude additional occult disease.  
3. Pathology review – Obtain tumour grade, lymphovascular/perineural invasion, and margin status from the primary specimen; these will refine postoperative risk assessment.  
4. Adjuvant systemic therapy – After recovery (typically 4–6 weeks), initiate adjuvant chemotherapy. Given RAS‑wild‑type status, a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (e.g., CAPOX or FOLFOX) is standard; consider adding an anti‑EGFR agent (cetuximab) if the primary is high‑risk (poor differentiation, T4, N2) and the patient tolerates it.  
5. Surveillance – Serial CEA measurements every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months, combined with contrast‑enhanced CT (or MRI if available) of chest/abdomen at 6‑month intervals.  
6. Contingency planning – If intra‑operative assessment reveals insufficient FLR or unexpected vascular involvement, abort hepatic resection, consider portal‑vein embolisation and a staged (liver‑first) approach, or postpone liver surgery until after systemic therapy.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumour (affects adjuvant‑therapy intensity).  
- Vascular or biliary involvement of the liver lesions (could alter the extent of hepatic resection needed).  
- Dedicated liver MRI (provides more accurate lesion mapping and vascular anatomy).  
- Formal FLR ratio calculation (confirms safety of hepatic resection).  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been given (would influence timing of surgery and choice of postoperative regimen).  

These missing items are the most critical to confirm before final operative planning, but none currently preclude proceeding with the recommended upfront combined resection.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases (segments II and V, 2.2 cm and 3 cm), bilobar but peripheral, without radiologic evidence of extrahepatic disease. Both lesions appear technically amenable to limited parenchymal-sparing resections (wedge/segmentectomy) with preservation of adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Priority: management of the symptomatic primary tumor
• The subocclusive presentation makes the left colonic lesion the immediate priority.
• Perform an oncologic left colectomy first (or ileostomy) with lymphadenectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) to treat the obstruction risk and allow safe continuation of the oncologic strategy.
• Alternative : consider a temporary diversion before colectomy according to exact degree of subocclusion.

B. Early systemic therapy after recovery from colectomy
• After the emergent procedure, perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise 
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
• Initiate peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• Given the high CEA level (120 ng/mL), the situation suggests biologically active disease; short-course neoadjuvant therapy allows treatment of micrometastases and assessment of tumor biology.
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT decision and tolerance.

C. Liver surgery after restaging (liver-first not indicated here due to symptoms)
• After 2–3 months of chemotherapy, perform high-resolution liver MRI and CT restaging.
• If stability or response is observed, proceed to parenchymal-sparing liver resections: segment II wedge/segmentectomy and segment V wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound.
• Aim for R0 margins (>1mm) while preserving maximal liver parenchyma.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Post-hepatectomy therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including pre-operative cycles).
• Close postoperative surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially high tumor marker level.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact degree of subocclusion and whether an temporary diversion is required before colectomy.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of both metastases to confirm feasibility of parenchymal-sparing resections.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Exact location of the left colon tumor (descending vs sigmoid) influencing surgical planning.
E. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
F. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
G. Perform liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The case shows a solitary 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI (LiverMetastasesCharacterization → NumberOfMetastases = 1; MaximumLesionDiameter = 2.5 cm) with no extra‑hepatic disease (Extrahepatic → False). Technically this lesion is amenable to a limited segmentectomy, which would usually meet the criteria of preserving ≥2 contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow. However, key information required to confirm surgical feasibility is missing: liver MRI (LiverMetastasesImagingExams → Has liver MRI been performed? Missing), precise vascular/biliary relationship (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion → Missing; ArterialAnatomy → Missing), and the future liver remnant volume ratio (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio → Missing). Because these missing data are decisive for confirming that a safe resection can be performed, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the required assessments.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Diagnostic work‑up  
  – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase to delineate the lesion’s relationship to hepatic vessels, bile ducts and to calculate the FLR volume.  
  – Perform a full colonoscopic assessment of the primary tumor and document any obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms (ColorectalPrimaryTumorSymptomatology → Missing).  

• Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
  – Because the metastasis is synchronous and the primary harbors a KRAS mutation, initiate 4–6 cycles of an oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) – the regimen supported for KRAS‑mutated disease and shown to increase conversion and R0 rates in the literature.  
  – Re‑stage with repeat imaging (CT + MRI) after chemotherapy to confirm that the lesion remains resectable and that FLR is adequate.  

• Surgical sequencing (once resectability is confirmed)  
  – If the primary tumor is asymptomatic and the liver lesion remains resectable after chemotherapy, proceed with a simultaneous (combined) operation: right hemicolectomy (or extended right hemicolectomy as required) together with a segment VI anatomical resection (or wedge resection with negative margin). Simultaneous resection is justified because the hepatic procedure is limited (≤ 3 segments) and avoids a second major operation.  
  – If the primary tumor is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or if intra‑operative assessment reveals insufficient FLR, adopt a liver‑first (reverse) approach: first perform the segmentectomy after chemotherapy, then address the colon primary after recovery.  

• Post‑operative management  
  – Pathology review of margins; aim for R0 resection.  
  – Resume adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of 6 months total peri‑operative therapy) based on tolerance.  
  – Follow‑up with CEA monitoring and periodic imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
The most critical missing items that must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be made are:  
- Liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (to assess vascular/biliary involvement and calculate FLR).  
- Quantified future liver remnant ratio (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery).  
- Confirmation of whether the primary colorectal tumor has already been resected (ColorectalPrimaryTumorPostResectionCharacterization → Missing) and its symptom status (obstruction, perforation, bleeding).  
- Detailed arterial anatomy and any vascular contact of the metastasis (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion, ArterialAnatomy).  

Acquiring these data will allow conversion of the “Potentially resectable” classification to “Resectable upfront” and enable definitive surgical planning.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the solitary 1.8 cm segment III metastasis is technically amenable to a minor hepatectomy (segmentectomy) and the rectal primary is amenable to total mesorectal excision after short‑course radiotherapy. However, definitive classification cannot be made until (a) a complete thoraco‑abdominal staging CT (or CT chest + CT abdomen/pelvis) is performed to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease, and (b) cross‑sectional liver imaging (contrast‑enhanced MRI or multiphase CT) is obtained to confirm absence of vascular or biliary involvement and to calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. These missing pieces are decisive for surgical feasibility.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Staging phase  
 – Obtain a thoraco‑CT (or chest CT) and a contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT or liver‑specific MRI to document the liver lesion’s relationship to vessels/bile ducts and to assess FLR.  
 – Review pathology of the rectal biopsy (grade) and confirm RAS‑wild type status (already known).  

• Neoadjuvant phase for the rectal primary  
 – Deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) as already planned.  
 – During the 2‑week interval, consider a short course of peri‑operative systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 2–3 cycles of FOLFOX) as a “test‑of‑time” to assess tumor biology; this is optional given the low metastatic burden but is supported by guidelines for synchronous disease.  

• Restaging (≈4–6 weeks after RT)  
 – Repeat pelvic MRI to evaluate tumor response and circumferential margin.  
 – Repeat liver imaging to confirm that the metastasis remains resectable and that FLR is adequate (>30 % in a normal liver, >40 % if steatosis).  

• Surgical sequencing (based on restaging)  
 Option A – Simultaneous (combined) approach (preferred if liver resection is limited to segment III and the patient’s operative risk is acceptable):  
  – Laparoscopic left‑lateral segmentectomy (segment III) with intra‑operative ultrasound to verify margins.  
  – Low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision 6–8 weeks after radiotherapy (or in the same session if operative time and patient condition allow), with a diverting loop ileostomy.  

 Option B – Liver‑first (reverse) approach (if rectal symptoms develop or if a brief interval after RT is desired):  
  – Perform laparoscopic segment III resection 1–2 weeks after completion of short‑course RT.  
  – Proceed with TME 6–8 weeks later, after confirming no progression of the primary.  

• Post‑operative management  
 – Pathology review of both specimens (R0 margin required).  
 – Resume adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX) based on final pathology and patient tolerance.  
 – Consider adjuvant radiotherapy if the rectal margin is close (<1 mm) or if there is residual disease.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Thoraco‑CT (or chest imaging) to rule out pulmonary metastases – essential to confirm that disease is liver‑only.  
• Abdominal CT or liver‑specific MRI – required to define vascular/biliary involvement, exact size, and to calculate the FLR ratio.  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to ensure safe hepatic resection.  
• Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor – influences prognosis and may affect the aggressiveness of systemic therapy.  
• Confirmation of whether the primary tumor has already been resected – determines whether a simultaneous or staged approach is feasible.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis located in segment III. The lesion seems technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for solitary, small metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial liver anatomy. 

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and rectum MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N1 upper rectal tumor with limited parietal invasion, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the single segment III lesion using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segment III metastasis followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the single segment III metastasis, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
B. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT . Chest CT.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
D. Detailed relationship of the liver lesion to segment III vascular structures on liver MRI.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 72 years old, discovery at abdominal CT scan of a transverse colon adenocarcinoma, CEA 410 ng/mL, three liver metastases (segments IV, V and VI) measuring 2 to 3 cm. Liver MRI: partial contact with the right portal branch without invasion. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable metastases, simple liver surgery possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The liver lesions are limited (3 cm ≤ size, 3 lesions in segments IV‑V‑VI) and imaging shows only partial contact with the right portal branch without frank invasion, which makes a margin‑negative, non‑anatomic resection technically feasible. However, the structured analysis lacks a documented future liver remnant (FLR) ratio, and FLR adequacy is a decisive functional criterion for safe hepatectomy. In addition, thoracic imaging to rule out pulmonary metastases is missing. Because these key pieces of information are absent, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront” and must be considered potentially resectable pending confirmation of adequate FLR (or need for portal vein embolisation) and exclusion of extra‑hepatic disease.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging  
  • Obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude lung metastases.  
  • Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate the FLR ratio; if FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy) plan portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage approach.  
- Neoadjuvant systemic therapy  
  • Start peri‑operative chemotherapy (e.g., 3–4 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumour is KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents not indicated) and the CEA is markedly elevated (410 ng/mL), suggesting aggressive biology.  
  • Use this interval to assess disease biology (“proof of time”) and to monitor for progression of any occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
  • Repeat liver MRI and FLR volumetry; confirm that all three metastases remain resectable with negative margins and that the FLR is sufficient.  
  • If FLR remains inadequate, proceed with PVE and re‑image after hypertrophy.  
- Surgical sequencing  
  • If the primary transverse colon tumour is asymptomatic and the patient’s performance status permits, a simultaneous resection (right hemicolectomy + non‑anatomic wedge resections of segments IV, V, VI) can be performed, prioritising the liver resection first to control metastatic disease.  
  • If the primary tumour is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding) or the patient’s operative risk is high, adopt a staged approach: (1) liver‑first resection after confirming FLR, followed by (2) colon resection after recovery.  
- Post‑operative management  
  • Complete peri‑operative chemotherapy to a total of 6 months (or longer per MDT decision).  
  • Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT chest/abdomen) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio or volumetric assessment.  
- Thoracic imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Status of the primary colorectal tumour (resected vs. unresected, presence of obstruction, perforation or bleeding).  
- Detailed arterial anatomy of the liver (to plan safe inflow control).  
- Confirmation of absence of bone or brain metastases (currently “Missing”).  

These items must be obtained before definitive surgical planning can be finalized.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, T3N1 sigmoid colon tumor associated with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) at the abdominal CT scan. Maximum size: 2.9 cm. CEA 200 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, HER2 negative.
MDT Discussion: Primarily resectable lesions, no vascular or extra-hepatic involvement.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Four peripheral metastases (segments II, III, V, VIII) ≤ 3 cm, no vascular contact → technically amenable to parenchymal‑sparing wedge/segmental resections.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease identified on the limited imaging performed.  
- However, the Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio is not reported; adequacy of FLR is a decisive factor for safe hepatectomy (criterion 4 of modern resectability definitions).  
- The status of the primary sigmoid tumor (resected or not) is also missing, which influences the need for simultaneous versus staged resection.  
Because a specific prerequisite (confirmation of an adequate FLR, and clarification of primary‑tumor status) is required before definitive surgery, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Obtain a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or high‑quality multiphase CT) to delineate lesion borders, vascular anatomy, and to plan parenchymal‑sparing resections.  
   - Perform a thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases.  
   - Calculate FLR volume using volumetric software; target >30 % of total liver volume in a chemotherapy‑naïve liver (or >40 % if prior chemotherapy is planned).  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (if FLR borderline or to assess tumor biology)  
   - Give 3 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab) because the tumor is RAS‑wild‑type.  
   - Re‑measure CEA and restage with MRI/CT after chemotherapy; a response or stable disease supports proceeding to surgery, while progression would prompt alternative strategies.  

3. Surgical planning  
   - If primary tumor has not yet been resected and the patient is fit: plan a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy (oncologic resection with adequate lymphadenectomy) and parenchymal‑sparing liver resections (wedge or segmental) to achieve R0 margins while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments.  
   - If primary tumor is already resected: proceed with liver‑only surgery as above.  
   - If FLR is insufficient after volumetry: consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in one lobe, PVE of the diseased lobe, second stage: resection of the hypertrophied remnant).  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Adjuvant chemotherapy (completion of a 6‑month peri‑operative regimen) to address micrometastatic disease.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance per standard guidelines.  

Step 3 – Missing data (most crucial for the recommendation)  
- Future Liver Remnant (FLR) ratio / volumetric assessment.  
- Liver MRI (or high‑resolution multiphase CT) to define lesion anatomy and vascular relationships.  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult pulmonary metastases.  
- Status of the primary sigmoid tumor (already resected or still in situ).  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (affects risk stratification).  
- Presence of obstructive, perforative, or bleeding symptoms from the primary lesion.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four peripheral liver metastases (segments II, III, V, and VIII), all smaller than 3 cm, without vascular involvement or extrahepatic disease. The distribution is bilobar but the lesions are technically amenable to multiple parenchymal-sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and peripheral location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (recommended)
• The elevated CEA level (200 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Given the high CEA level (200 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI).
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy according to MDT decision.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segments II–III resections (left lateral section wedges).
– Segment V wedge resection.
– Segment VIII wedge resection.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed liver MRI describing vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 63 years old, right-sided T4N2M1 colon cancer, two liver metastases in segments II and IVa (3 and 4 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. Liver MRI: middle hepatic vein preserved. CEA 95 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable metastases, with priority given to controlling the primary tumor.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The liver lesions (3 cm and 4 cm in segments II and IVa, middle hepatic vein preserved) are described as technically resectable, and no extra‑hepatic disease is identified. However, the structured analysis lacks two decisive pieces of information that directly determine surgical feasibility:  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio (FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing).  
- Presence of vascular contact or invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion = Missing).  

Because these items are required to confirm that an R0 resection can be performed while preserving adequate liver function, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending acquisition of the missing data.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Complete pre‑operative staging  
   - Review colonoscopy and pathology to confirm primary tumor resectability; obtain histologic grade (currently Missing).  
   - Perform volumetric CT or MRI to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % (or < 20 % in compromised liver) plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   - Re‑evaluate vascular anatomy (arterial/portal/venous) and any tumor‑vessel contact on high‑resolution imaging.  

2. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
   - Initiate 4–6 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX) or triplet (FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status and elevated CEA (95 ng/mL).  
   - Use response assessment (RECIST) after chemotherapy to confirm disease stability or regression; progression would defer surgery.  

3. Surgical sequencing  
   - Because the MDT indicated priority to control the primary tumor and the primary is right‑sided colon cancer, plan a primary‑first approach if the colon lesion is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation) or if the primary is easily resectable.  
   - If the primary is asymptomatic and the FLR is adequate after chemotherapy, a simultaneous resection (right hemicolectomy + left lateral/segment IVa hepatectomy) is feasible, as the liver resection involves ≤ 3 segments and preserves two contiguous segments.  
   - If FLR is insufficient after chemotherapy, perform PVE, wait 4–6 weeks for hypertrophy, then proceed with liver resection (either staged after primary resection or as a delayed liver‑first operation).  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Complete a total of 6 months of peri‑operative systemic therapy (including postoperative adjuvant cycles).  
   - Monitor CEA serially; aim for postoperative CEA < 5 ng/mL.  
   - Schedule surveillance imaging (CT chest/abdomen) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  

- Future liver remnant (FLR) volume/ratio – required to confirm that hepatic resection will leave sufficient functional liver.  
- Vascular contact or invasion – determines whether an R0 resection is technically achievable without complex vascular reconstruction.  
- Primary tumor resection status and symptomatology (obstruction, perforation, bleeding) – dictates whether a primary‑first or simultaneous approach is indicated.  
- Histologic grade of differentiation – influences prognosis and may affect the aggressiveness of systemic therapy.  
- Timing of liver metastases (synchronous vs. metachronous) – impacts the choice between liver‑first, primary‑first, or simultaneous strategies.  
- Whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered – informs the need for additional neoadjuvant cycles and helps assess tumor biology.  

Acquiring these missing items will allow conversion from “Potentially resectable” to a definitive “Resectable upfront” or, if unfavorable, to “Not resectable.”

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The three liver metastases are small (1‑2 cm) and confined to segments VI‑VIII, making a right‑posterior segmentectomy technically feasible. However, decisive information is missing: a dedicated liver MRI (to confirm lesion number, vascular/biliary relationships and rule out additional occult disease) and an explicit future liver remnant (FLR) ratio calculation. Without these data the safety of hepatic resection cannot be confirmed, so resection must be preceded by the missing imaging and FLR assessment (or a confirming portal‑vein embolisation plan if FLR is inadequate).

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) for the upper‑rectal T3N0 primary (as already planned by the MDT).  
• Within 2‑3 weeks after radiotherapy, obtain restaging studies:  
   – Pelvic MRI to evaluate circumferential resection margin, mesorectal fascia involvement and response of the primary.  
   – Multiphasic liver MRI with liver‑specific contrast to verify the three lesions, assess vascular/biliary contact, and detect any additional metastases.  
   – Thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude pulmonary disease (brain MRI if clinically indicated).  
• Calculate FLR volume from the imaging; if FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.4 % of body weight) proceed; if FLR is insufficient, consider right‑portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
• Surgical sequence (based on MDT suggestion of “combined treatment after short‑course RT”):  
   1. Perform simultaneous curative‑intent surgery 6‑8 weeks after radiotherapy:  
      – Total mesorectal excision (TME) with a protective diverting stoma as indicated.  
      – Anatomical segmentectomy of segments VI‑VIII (right‑posterior sectionectomy) achieving R0 margins, preserving at least two contiguous left‑liver segments.  
   2. If intra‑operative assessment reveals inadequate FLR, abort hepatic resection, place portal‑vein embolisation, and schedule delayed liver surgery.  
• Peri‑operative systemic therapy: given RAS‑wild‑type status, offer peri‑operative FOLFOX (± anti‑EGFR such as cetuximab) – either 3 cycles pre‑operatively (conversion/biologic test of disease biology) or, if the liver resection proceeds without neoadjuvant chemotherapy, give 3–6 cycles adjuvant post‑operative chemotherapy.  
• Post‑operative management: monitor CEA, repeat liver MRI and chest CT at 3‑6 month intervals, consider adjuvant radiotherapy to the pelvis only if pathological risk factors (e.g., positive CRM) are present.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Liver MRI (vascular/biliary involvement, occult lesions).  
• FLR ratio calculation (volumetric assessment).  
• Thoracic CT (or complete chest imaging) to rule out pulmonary metastases.  
• Status of primary‑tumor resection (has it already been removed? – needed for surgical planning).  
• Grade of differentiation of the rectal primary (affects need for intensified systemic therapy).  
• Information on any systemic chemotherapy already administered (to decide on further peri‑operative cycles).  
These missing items are essential to confirm that a safe, curative‑intent hepatic resection can be performed and to finalize the sequencing of systemic and local therapies.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, history of hypertension, discovery of left colon cancer and a single 2.7 cm liver metastasis in segment IVb at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 40 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, anatomically favorable for a single resection.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The liver disease consists of a single 2.7 cm metastasis in segment IVb, with no extra‑hepatic lesions on CT. A solitary peripheral lesion of this size is technically amenable to a limited segmental resection while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. The primary tumour is located in the left colon, which is generally compatible with a simultaneous colorectal resection. Molecular profile (BRAF wild‑type, MSS) and low tumour burden further support curative intent without the need for down‑staging.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• Complete pre‑operative staging:  
   – Perform liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT volumetry) to confirm lesion anatomy, vascular/biliary relationships and calculate FLR ratio.  
   – Chest CT/PET‑CT to reconfirm absence of pulmonary disease.  
   – Full colonoscopic assessment of the primary tumour, obtain biopsy if not already done, and assess for obstruction, perforation or bleeding.  
   – Optimize comorbidities (blood pressure control, nutritional status, ECOG 0‑1).  

• Multidisciplinary decision: given confirmed resectability, plan a simultaneous resection (colon + liver) because the patient is fit (70 y, hypertension only) and there are no symptoms requiring staged priority.  

• Surgical plan:  
   – Laparoscopic (or open if required) left‑sided colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy.  
   – Intra‑operative ultrasound of the liver, followed by a segment IVb non‑anatomical/segmental resection with ≥1 cm margins.  
   – Ensure preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments and a FLR > 30 % (expected after a single‑segment resection).  
   – Use Pringle maneuver only if needed; avoid excessive inflow occlusion to limit ischemic injury.  

• Post‑operative management:  
   – Standard enhanced recovery pathway, monitor liver function.  
   – Pathology review of primary (grade, margins, nodal status) and metastasis.  
   – Adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX ± biologic) given the presence of synchronous disease, even though the risk profile is favourable.  
   – Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT or MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumour (affects need for adjuvant therapy).  
- Confirmation that the primary tumour has not already been resected (impacts sequencing).  
- Detailed vascular/biliary involvement of the liver lesion (critical for technical feasibility).  
- Liver MRI and FLR volumetric assessment (required to verify that the future liver remnant is sufficient).  
- Whether any obstructive, perforative or bleeding symptoms are present from the primary tumour (would dictate staged versus simultaneous approach).  
- Any prior systemic therapy (could influence liver parenchymal quality and postoperative liver failure risk).

The lesion is anatomically favorable for a a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. • Perform high-resolution liver MRI to confirm the relationship of the lesion to segment IVb vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection.

• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology, however the KRAS status is unknown.

• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT.

• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment IVb wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles).

   - Calculate FLR volume (CT‑volumetry) and compare with the 30 % (chemotherapy‑naïve) or 40 % (post‑chemotherapy) threshold.

- Initiate conversion systemic therapy: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease excludes anti‑EGFR agents). Deliver at least 4 cycles (≈2 months), then restage with triphasic CT and liver‑specific MRI.

If the primary remains symptomatic or margins are threatened, consider short‑course radiotherapy before TME.

Woman, 55 years old, left T3N2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases, some coalescent in the hilar region at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, maximum size 5.5 cm. CEA 800 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.

Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- The liver disease is extensive (7 metastases, largest 5.5 cm, some coalescent in the hilar region) – a situation that typically exceeds “upfront resectable” criteria (requires at least two contiguous segments, adequate inflow/outflow and sufficient future liver remnant).  
- Critical technical information is missing: hepatic segments involved, presence of vascular or biliary invasion, and the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. Without these data a safe upfront resection cannot be confirmed.  
- The MDT already labeled the case “borderline” and suggested a two‑stage hepatectomy after effective chemotherapy, indicating that downsizing and/or hypertrophy are expected prerequisites.  
- Therefore a specific prerequisite action (pre‑operative systemic chemotherapy with subsequent imaging and FLR assessment) is required before a definitive surgical plan can be made, fitting the definition of “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Systemic therapy (induction chemotherapy)  
   - Initiate an intensive regimen (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab) because the disease is synchronous, KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents not indicated), and tumor burden is high (CEA 800 ng/mL).  
   - Treat for 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles), reassessing response with RECIST criteria after each two‑cycle interval.  

2. Restaging work‑up  
   - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with diffusion‑weighted sequences to define lesion number, exact segmental distribution, vascular/biliary involvement, and to detect any occult disease.  
   - Conduct volumetric CT or MRI to calculate the FLR; aim for FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver (or ≥ 40 % if steatosis is present after chemotherapy).  

3. Decision point after chemotherapy  
   - If sufficient tumor shrinkage (e.g., reduction in size or number, especially of the hilar cluster) and FLR is adequate, proceed to a single‑stage curative resection (possible if the remaining disease can be cleared while preserving ≥ 2 contiguous segments).  
   - If FLR is insufficient or the hilar lesions remain borderline, plan a two‑stage hepatectomy:  
     a. Stage 1 – resect lesions confined to the future liver remnant side (e.g., left lateral sectionectomy) and perform right portal vein embolization (PVE) to induce hypertrophy of the left lobe.  
     b. Interval – wait 4–6 weeks, repeat volumetry to confirm FLR growth to the target threshold.  
     c. Stage 2 – complete resection of the remaining right‑lobe disease (right hepatectomy or extended right resection) ensuring negative margins (R0).  

4. Management of the primary colon tumor  
   - Verify whether the primary has already been resected (Missing item).  
   - If not resected and the patient is asymptomatic, a liver‑first approach is reasonable: treat liver disease as above, then perform a standard left‑sided colectomy (segmental or hemicolectomy) after hepatic clearance.  
   - If the primary is symptomatic (obstruction, bleeding, perforation – currently Missing/Assumed False), address it first (primary‑first strategy) before or concurrent with systemic therapy.  

5. Adjuvant/maintenance therapy  
   - After complete hepatic and colorectal resection, resume postoperative chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to treat microscopic disease and reduce recurrence risk.  

6. Surveillance  
   - Serial CEA measurements every 3 months and cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, to detect early recurrence.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Grade of differentiation of the primary tumor (affects biological risk).  
- Whether the primary colon cancer has already been surgically resected.  
- Presence of obstructive, perforative, or bleeding symptoms from the primary.  
- Detailed hepatic segment involvement, vascular contact/invasion, and biliary involvement.  
- Pre‑treatment liver MRI results.  
- Results of any systemic therapy already given (if any).  
- Exact future liver remnant (FLR) ratio and volumetric data.  
These missing items are essential to confirm technical resectability, to choose between a single‑stage versus two‑stage hepatic approach, and to finalize the sequencing of primary‑tumor surgery.

Potentially resectable – The case presents extensive bilobar liver involvement (5 lesions in segments II, III, IVa, VI, VII) and a primary rectal T3N1 tumor that has not yet been resected. These missing, decisive pieces of information place the patient in the “potentially resectable” category.

- Surveillance: CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3‑6 months for the first 2 years.

- Post‑operative (adjuvant) therapy

   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.

- Confirmation that the primary sigmoid colon cancer has already been resected and that no obstructive/bleeding symptoms are present.  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) volumetric assessment.  
- History of any prior systemic chemotherapy for the metastasis (to decide whether neoadjuvant therapy is needed).

Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
- Classification: Potentially resectable  
- Reasoning:  
  • The structured analysis shows 4 bilobar liver metastases (NumberOfMetastases = 4; MaximumLesionDiameter = 3.5 cm) that are metachronous (Timing = Metachronous) and the patient has no radiologically evident pulmonary disease (ExtrahepaticPulmonaryInvolvement = False).  
  • MDT comment states “potentially resectable based on volumetric assessment,” indicating that technical feasibility hinges on liver remnant volume and possibly on tumor‑vascular relationships.  
  • Critical technical data are missing: FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery (Missing), HepaticSegmentsInvolved (Missing), PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion (Missing), and arterial anatomy (Missing). Without a confirmed adequate future liver remnant (≥30 % in a normal liver) or confirmation that major vessels are not involved, an upfront operation cannot be safely planned.  
  • Therefore a prerequisite step (assessment/optimization of FLR or clarification of vascular involvement) is required before definitive surgery, fulfilling the definition of “Potentially resectable.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline systemic therapy  
   - Initiate 3–4 cycles of a standard doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPOX) with a biologic agent (anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR, given BRAF wild‑type and left‑sided primary).  
   - Goals: (a) assess tumor biology (“test of time”) given the markedly elevated CEA (380 ng/mL), (b) potentially down‑size lesions, and (c) treat micrometastatic disease.  

2. Re‑assessment after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat high‑quality liver MRI with hepatocyte‑specific contrast and a volumetric CT to:  
     • Determine the future liver remnant (FLR) ratio.  
     • Re‑evaluate vascular and biliary involvement.  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥40 % after extensive chemotherapy‑induced liver injury) and no major vascular invasion, proceed to surgery.  

3. Surgical planning  
   - If FLR is adequate:  
     • Perform a parenchymal‑sparing, margin‑negative (R0) hepatectomy.  
     • Because disease is bilobar, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy (e.g., right portal vein embolization/ligation followed by delayed contralateral resection) or a simultaneous resection if the combined operative time is acceptable and the patient’s performance status permits.  
   - If FLR is insufficient:  
     • Undertake portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, then re‑operate once FLR reaches safe limits.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (e.g., total of 6 months peri‑operative therapy) as adjuvant treatment, guided by postoperative CEA trend.  
   - Surveillance: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years.  

Step 3 – Missing data most crucial for the recommendation  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – needed to decide whether a single‑stage resection is safe or whether PVE/ALPPS is required.  
- Hepatic segment involvement and vascular/biliary contact – determines resectability margins and the need for complex vascular reconstruction.  
- Prior systemic therapy status – unknown whether the patient has already received chemotherapy; this influences the decision to give neoadjuvant treatment versus proceeding directly to surgery.  
- Performance status / comorbidities (e.g., cardiac, pulmonary, liver function) – essential for assessing operative risk.  
- Peritoneal and bone involvement – both marked as Missing; presence would convert the case to unresectable or require combined modality treatment.  
- Tumor grade, primary‑margin status, and CA 19‑9 level – absent but useful for prognostication and for refining the need for neoadjuvant therapy.  

Addressing these missing items will allow conversion from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four metachronous bilobar liver metastases (2–3.5 cm) without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Although distributed in both lobes, the limited number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited bilobar metachronous metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT to precisely define the segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships of the 4 lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) to confirm feasibility of a single-stage approach.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA level (380 ng/mL) and early recurrence (18 months), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the four lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound aiming for R0 margins.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of the four lesions on MRI with detailed vascular and biliary relationships of each lesion.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Details of any adjuvant chemotherapy received after the initial colectomy.
G. Exact CEA trend over time prior to detection of the lesion.
H. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA.
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma resected 3 years earlier. CEA 520 ng/mL. at the abdominal CT scan: two liver metastases (segments II and VI), sizes 3.1 and 4.0 cm. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous liver recurrence, anatomically possible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The two liver lesions (3.1 cm in segment II and 4.0 cm in segment VI) are anatomically amenable to resection, but key information required to confirm safe hepatectomy is missing. The structured analysis lacks thoracic CT (to exclude pulmonary metastases), liver MRI (to define vascular/biliary involvement and precise tumor borders), and a calculated future liver remnant (FLR) ratio. In addition, the patient has high‑risk oncologic features (CEA 520 ng/mL, KRAS mutation, right‑sided primary, bilobar disease, lesion >3 cm) that usually prompt neoadjuvant systemic therapy before definitive surgery. Because these missing data and the need for pre‑operative chemotherapy are decisive for surgical feasibility, the case is classified as “Potentially resectable.”

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging: obtain a thoracic CT scan and a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (preferably with hepatocyte‑specific agent) to rule out extra‑hepatic disease and to assess vascular/biliary involvement of the metastases.  
- Perform volumetric liver assessment on the MRI (or CT) to calculate the FLR; aim for an FLR ≥ 30 % in a normal liver or ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected.  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOXIRI ± bevacizumab) given the KRAS‑mutated status, very high CEA, and bilobar disease. This serves both as a biological test (“proof of time”) and may downsize the lesions.  
- Re‑image after chemotherapy (CT/MRI) to evaluate tumor response, confirm that the lesions remain resectable, and re‑calculate the FLR.  
- If disease is stable or responding and FLR is adequate, proceed to curative liver surgery: perform a non‑anatomic wedge resection of segment II and a segment VI resection (or anatomical segmentectomy) in a single operation, preserving at least two contiguous segments of functional liver. No simultaneous colorectal surgery is needed because the primary has already been removed.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy (or longer per multidisciplinary recommendation).  
- Surveillance: CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of chest and abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Thoracic CT scan (to exclude pulmonary metastases).  
- Liver MRI with vascular/biliary assessment (to define lesion anatomy and involvement).  
- Calculated FLR ratio (to ensure safe hepatic reserve).  
- Confirmation of whether any systemic chemotherapy has already been administered.  
These missing items are the most critical for finalizing resectability and planning the surgical approach.

Case_Content:
Man, 60 years old, right colectomy for T3N1 tumor 2 years ago. CEA 140 ng/mL. Liver MRI: three liver metastases (IV, V, VI), sizes 2 to 3 cm. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Limited liver involvement, no other locations.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
• Classification: Potentially resectable  
• Reasoning: The three metachronous liver metastases (2‑3 cm) are located in segments IV, V and VI, a distribution that can be addressed with parenchymal‑sparing segmental resections while preserving at least two contiguous segments. However, the structured analysis lacks two decisive pieces of information:  
   – Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – not reported; an FLR < 20‑30 % (depending on liver quality) would preclude safe resection.  
   – Presence of vascular or biliary involvement – also missing; invasion of major hepatic veins, portal or hepatic artery branches could make an R0 resection technically impossible.  
Because these missing data directly determine whether a curative hepatectomy can be performed, the case must be considered potentially resectable pending confirmation of adequate FLR and absence of critical vascular/biliary contact.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging work‑up  
   – Obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis (or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease (especially bone, which is listed as missing).  
   – Perform volumetric liver CT or MRI to calculate the FLR ratio and assess vascular anatomy (arterial, portal, hepatic veins).  
2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (given high CEA = 140 ng/mL and to test tumor biology)  
   – Initiate 2–3 months of a doublet regimen (FOLFOX) combined with an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type.  
   – Re‑measure CEA after each cycle and repeat liver MRI to document response and ensure no progression.  
3. Re‑assessment  
   – If imaging shows stable or regressed lesions and FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 20 % with normal liver parenchyma), proceed to surgery.  
   – If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the future remnant; repeat volumetry 3‑4 weeks later.  
4. Surgical plan  
   – Perform parenchymal‑sparing segmental resections: segment IV (left medial) and segments V + VI (right posterior) with intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins. Aim for R0 (≥ 1 mm) resection while preserving at least two contiguous segments (e.g., segments II‑III‑VII‑VIII).  
   – Use intra‑operative ultrasound and, if needed, limited radiofrequency ablation for any sub‑centimeter satellite lesions not amenable to resection.  
5. Post‑operative management  
   – Resume the same systemic regimen (or switch to a maintenance protocol) for a total of 6 months of peri‑operative chemotherapy, as supported by the Nordlinger et al. trial showing improved progression‑free survival with peri‑operative FOLFOX.  
   – Monitor CEA monthly; a decreasing trend post‑resection predicts favorable prognosis.  
   – Schedule surveillance imaging (CT or MRI) every 3‑4 months for the first 2 years.

Step 3 – Missing data  
• Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio – essential to confirm that enough functional liver will remain after resection.  
• Vascular and biliary involvement of the metastases – needed to determine whether an R0 resection is technically feasible.  
• Confirmation of absence of bone metastases (currently “Missing”) – required to rule out extra‑hepatic disease that would alter the curative intent.  
• Details of prior systemic therapy (if any) and liver function tests – important for planning neoadjuvant chemotherapy and assessing risk of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
These items must be obtained before finalizing the surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 74 years old, rectal cancer resected 5 years ago, new CEA elevation to 600 ng/mL. at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: single liver metastasis segment IVa (4.2 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late solitary metastasis, potentially curable situation.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The structured analysis confirms a solitary 4.2 cm metastasis in segment IVa (NumberOfMetastases = 1, MaximumLesionDiameter = 4.2 cm, HepaticSegmentsInvolved = IVa) with no extra‑hepatic disease on CT (ExtrahepaticPulmonaryInvolvement = False, Peritoneal = Assumed False, LymphNode = False). Technically this lesion is amenable to an anatomic or non‑anatomic resection. However, the analysis lists several decisive missing items:  

- FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing (required to ensure that removal of segment IVa leaves ≥ 30 % functional liver).  
- PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion = Missing (needed to plan safe transection and to decide if vascular reconstruction is required).  
- LiverMRIPerformed = Missing (gold‑standard imaging to define lesion borders, vascular anatomy and to calculate FLR).  

Because these pieces of information are essential for confirming that a curative R0 resection can be performed safely, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” No oncological contraindication (e.g., extensive extra‑hepatic disease) is present, so the lesion is not “Not resectable.” Hence the appropriate category is “Potentially resectable” – resection will be possible after obtaining the missing technical data and, preferably, after a short course of systemic therapy to assess tumor biology.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Complete staging  
   - Perform a contrast‑enhanced liver MRI with hepatobiliary phase to delineate the lesion, assess vascular/biliary involvement, and obtain volumetric data for future liver remnant (FLR).  
   - Calculate FLR volume (CT or MRI volumetry) and confirm that FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is suspected).  
   - Obtain a brain MRI (the only extra‑hepatic site labeled “Missing”) to rule out occult CNS disease; this is low priority but completes staging.  

2. Systemic therapy (neoadjuvant)  
   - Initiate peri‑operative chemotherapy because the CEA is markedly elevated (600 ng/mL) and the tumour is KRAS‑mutated (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective). A standard doublet such as FOLFOX ± bevacizumab for 3–4 cycles is appropriate.  
   - Re‑image (CT/MRI) after chemotherapy to verify that the liver lesion remains solitary, unchanged or reduced in size, and that no new lesions have appeared (biological “test‑of‑time”).  

3. Surgical planning  
   - If FLR is adequate and no vascular invasion is identified, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection. For a segment IVa lesion, options include a limited segmentectomy or a left lateral sectionectomy, aiming for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm).  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm the absence of additional occult lesions.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy post‑operatively (total of 6 months peri‑operative therapy) to address micrometastatic disease.  
   - Monitor CEA every 3 months and perform cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  

5. Multidisciplinary follow‑up  
   - Continue MDT review throughout treatment to reassess resectability if any progression occurs and to consider alternative locoregional therapies (e.g., thermal ablation or SBRT) if surgery becomes unsafe.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Future liver remnant (FLR) ratio/volumetry – essential to confirm that resection will leave sufficient functional liver.  
- Liver MRI with vascular and biliary assessment – required to define lesion borders, detect vascular contact/invasion, and provide accurate FLR calculation.  
- Presence of vascular or biliary involvement – influences the need for more extensive resection or vascular reconstruction.  
- Status of systemic therapy prior to surgery – currently “Missing”; a short neoadjuvant course is recommended to gauge tumour biology.  
- Brain imaging – the only extra‑hepatic site marked “Missing”; needed for complete staging, although less critical for immediate hepatic surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with a single metachronous liver metastasis in segment IVa (4.2 cm), without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Despite its central location, the lesion is technically amenable to a parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for late solitary, anatomically accessible metastasis, this pattern is considered resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI to precisely define vascular and biliary relationships.
• Given the high CEA level (600 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to confirm absence of additional occult lesions.

B. Surgical management upfront
• Given the long disease-free interval and isolated liver involvement, immediate surgical resection is appropriate without mandatory neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
• Perform a segment IVa wedge/segmentectomy guided by intra-operative ultrasound aiming for R0 margins.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Initiate adjuvant doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic treatment.

D. Surveillance
• Close postoperative follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the segment IVa lesion on MRI.
B. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy.
D. Pathological details of rectal rectal specimen
E. Whether any adjuvant chemotherapy was administered after the initial rectal cancer treatment.

Man, 59 years old, left T3N1 colon cancer operated 3 years earlier. Surveillance: CEA 310 ng/mL. Liver MRI: segment VII lesion (3.8 cm) and small segment V lesion. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous liver recurrence, eligible for local treatment.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The liver lesions (segment VII 3.8 cm and a small segment V lesion) are limited in number (2) and location, suggesting technical feasibility of an R0 resection (Primary Tumor → left colon, Liver Metastases → Number = 2, Maximum Diameter = 3.8 cm, Hepatic Segments = V, VII).  
- However, decisive staging information is missing: thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease (ImagingExams → ThoracoCTScanPerformed = Missing) and a quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) assessment (FutureLiverRemnantFLRRatio → FLRRatioCompatibilitySurgery = Missing).  
- Because these pieces of information directly determine whether a curative hepatic resection can be safely performed, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of the missing studies.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- a. Complete staging – obtain a contrast‑enhanced thoraco‑abdominal CT (or PET‑CT) and perform liver volumetry (CT or MRI) to calculate FLR; repeat MRI to confirm absence of vascular or biliary invasion (PresenceOfVascularContactOrInvasion = Missing).  
- b. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy – given the markedly elevated CEA (310 ng/mL) and the presence of two lesions, administer 3–4 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± bevacizumab. This aligns with the “peri‑operative chemotherapy for resectable CRLM” principle and provides a “proof of time” for disease biology.  
- c. Restaging after chemotherapy – repeat liver MRI with volumetry; if FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % in steatotic livers) and no new extra‑hepatic disease, proceed to surgery. If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization before resection.  
- d. Surgical resection – perform an anatomic right posterior sectionectomy (segments VI‑VII) combined with a non‑anatomic wedge of segment V, aiming for R0 margins ≥ 1 cm. Preserve at least two contiguous segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage (technical resectability criteria).  
- e. Post‑operative management – resume systemic therapy (additional 3–6 cycles) as adjuvant treatment; monitor CEA every 3 months; schedule surveillance imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals.  
- f. Contingency – if extra‑hepatic disease is identified and is limited (e.g., solitary resectable lung nodule), incorporate multidisciplinary treatment (resection or stereotactic radiotherapy) before or after hepatic surgery as appropriate.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Thoraco‑CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Quantitative FLR assessment (volumetry) to confirm that a safe liver remnant will remain after resection.  
- Evaluation of vascular or biliary involvement of the hepatic lesions.  
- Documentation of prior systemic therapy (has any chemotherapy already been given?).  
- Patient’s performance status and comorbidities (cardiopulmonary fitness for major hepatectomy).

Case_Content:
Woman, 68 years old, T3N2 rectal tumor operated 4 years ago. CEA 78 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two metastases segments III and VI (2 and 2.6 cm), no extra-hepatic involvement.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, anatomically simple.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront – The patient has only two metachronous liver metastases (2 cm in segment III and 2.6 cm in segment VI) with no radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease. The lesions are small, anatomically simple, and located in separate lobes, allowing curative‑intent parenchymal‑sparing resections while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. No vascular or biliary invasion is reported, and the primary rectal cancer was resected 4 years ago with no current symptoms, making immediate hepatic surgery feasible without mandatory pre‑operative down‑staging.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
• 1. Confirm baseline staging: obtain a thoraco‑abdominal‑pelvic CT (or PET‑CT) to verify the absence of occult extra‑hepatic disease and to document the pulmonary and peritoneal status (although the structured analysis already records false for these sites).  
• 2. Molecular work‑up: test the primary tumour (or archived tissue) for RAS, BRAF, and MSI/dMMR status; this will guide adjuvant systemic therapy and may influence the need for targeted agents.  
• 3. Peri‑operative systemic therapy: because the disease is limited (≤ 3 lesions) and the patient is fit, either (a) proceed directly to surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX/XELOX) or (b) give a short course of neoadjuvant chemotherapy (3–4 cycles) to obtain “biologic proof of time” and to treat micrometastatic disease, then re‑resect. The choice can be individualized; many centres favour upfront resection when FLR is adequate and lesions are resectable.  
• 4. Surgical plan: perform a single‑stage, parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy – segment III wedge/segmentectomy and segment VI wedge/segmentectomy – either open or laparoscopic depending on surgeon expertise and patient factors. Ensure a negative (R0) margin (>1 mm) and preserve at least 30 % functional liver volume. Intra‑operative ultrasound should be used to confirm lesion location and exclude additional occult disease.

Man, 66 years old, right colectomy for T4N2M0 cancer 24 months ago. FDG-PET: four liver foci, 1.5-3.5 cm, no extra-hepatic. KRAS mutated.
